newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Brown opts for experience in BOE committee.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Brown opts for experience in BOE committee.

text.p: Britain's new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown opted for experience over politics on Monday when he appointed four respected, but neutral, economists to the Bank of England's monetary policy committee.
The four outsiders join civil servants from the newly independent Bank of England on a new committee which will decide the level of British interest rates at monthly meetings.

Brown appointed Professor Charles Goodhart from the London School of Economics, Dr DeAnne Julius, chief economist of British Airways, Sir Alan Budd, chief economic adviser at the Treasury, and Professor Willem Buiter of Cambridge University.
Brown said the four would bring a range of experience to the Bank's new committee.
Goodhart and Buiter are leading academics, Julius an industrialist and Budd a Whitehall mandarin with close ties to the previous Conservative government.
None is strongly associated with the Labour Party.
"They will bring not only recognised expertise in their own fields, but a breadth of experience of finance and industry to the making of monetary policy in this country," said Brown.
Leading figures in London's financial district welcomed the appointments and said their experience would give the new monetary regime the necessary credibility.

"They don't come from any particular school and are quite clearly independent of political consideration," said Bill Martin, co-director of economic research at UBS and a member of the government's think-tank, the Central Policy Review Staff, in the 1970s.
He said there had been fears that Brown might have loaded the committee with close political allies. "This is clearly unjusfied."
Brown announced the shake-up to the monetary policy structure last month, giving the Bank operational independence to set interest rates for the first time.
Other City figures said they were pleased the Chancellor had opted for weight and experience.

"These are middle-of-the-road, sensible economists with plenty of institutional and committee experience," said Geoffrey Dicks, economist at Natwest Markets and a former professor at the London Business School.
"The experience of these people will give the new committee the credibility it needs."

Goodhart, 60 and described by peers as the country's leading economist, worked for 17 years as a monetary adviser at the Bank of England, becoming chief adviser in 1980. He describes himself as politically neutral.
He and Buiter will take up their places on the committee when it meets for the first time to discuss interest rates on Thursday and Friday.
Buiter, was born in the Netherlands in 1949 and has been Professor of International Macroeconomics at Cambridge.
Contractual difficulties mean the other two members will join later in the year.
Julius' appointment will take effect from September 1. She has been chief economist at British Airways Plc since 1993 and chairwoman of British Airways Pension Investment Management Ltd.
Budd, 59, will be appointed when he leaves his post as Chief Economic Adviser to the Treasury.
There was some surprise that an economist closely linked to the previous Conservative administration was selected, although the appointment was welcomed.

"There is a general feeling that if (former Chancellor of the Exchequer) Kenneth Clarke the only ministerial success of the last government, then Sir Alan Budd is closely associated with him," said Dicks.
"He got there after Britain joined the ERM and was not blamed when we were forced out. The advice he has given over the last six years is as good as it gets."
